doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: State of jazz and its audience
title: Being a middle-aged white player in jazz
summary: Mandel calls the complaint an excuse, naming strong white players and arguing every artist must find something significant to say.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Recently I’ve had a couple of conversations with musicians — white fellas in their let’s say between 35 and 50, and they’ve made the comment that that’s not a good thing to be in the jazz world these days. Middle aged white. Does that comment — a quick response.

Well I think a lot of us feel like, as a middle aged white guy, it’s work to keep up with the changes in our world. But I don’t think that it’s a bad thing to be trying to do that. Are they saying that they don’t get respect from the musicians? Are you talking about musicians themselves?

And they feel like — I don’t know to me that sounds like an excuse. This is a music that comes out of an African-American basis. I’ve thought of it as an African-American gift to the world. And there’s always been very strong white musicians back to Adrian Rollini up to Steve Lacy, Tim Berne, Dave Douglas, Myra Melford who I was hanging out with last night or Marilyn Crispell, Maria Schneider, or middle aged white guys I mean there are a lot of players who are quite strong. Marty Erlich, somebody who I enjoy quite a lot. You have to do something with the music. You can’t just learn it and play it and expect people to — let’s see — expect to say something significant. I think that any artist, and maybe people who are 35 to 50 are coming to grips with this in a really mature way, you have to say something that’s of significance and you have to delve into yourself to find out what that is that you have to say. And it’s not just like the energy of a 25 year old. I’ve got the chops, I’ve got the breath, and now I’m going to play for an hour. It’s like well now what’s important to say? What do we have to say that’s lasting? And I think that that’s a challenge that comes to any artist in any art form in middle age. So I think that they come to grips with the challenges. What does it mean to be white in America

playing a music that comes from an African-American basis? What does it mean to be middle aged and to be devoted to an art form that seems to be giving back very little in the way of monetary support? What distinguishes my work from his work, whether he’s black, white, purple, Latin, whatever. And I think that those are difficult challenges that we have to face but I think that it’s an excuse to say well I’m white and I’m middle aged so nobody cares about me. Well then make me care about you, you know? Tell me your story. Tell me what’s really — because I’m white and middle aged so I would be interested in hearing what you have to say. We’re still the baby boomers, the white, middle aged baby boomers are still the big part of the demographic. If you can’t reach that demographic that’s a big audience. If you can’t reach them that means you’re failing in your art form. And that’s whether you’re a movie maker, a choreographer, a novelist or a jazz musician.
